newsitem.title: USA: Middle East off the U.S. campaign map.
newsitem.headline: Middle East off the U.S. campaign map.

text.p: In the race for the White House, foreign policy usually takes a back seat.
But in next week's election, international affairs are not even on the campaign bus.
That includes the Middle East, which the Clinton administration had once hoped to tout as a foreign policy success.

In his four years at the White House, President Bill Clinton has hosted three Arab-Israeli summits, visited Israel twice and sent his secretary of state, Warren Christopher, to the Middle East more than 20 times -- compared with once to Beijing.
Conventional wisdom had it that Clinton invested so much time and effort because he wanted Jewish funding for his Democratic party and the Jewish vote on November 5.
"He's already got it," said pollster John Zogby. "The majority of American Jews say they are going to vote for him."
Jews make up less than two percent of the electorate but they are concentrated in important electoral college states such as New York, Illinois, Pennsylvania, California and Florida.
This could be a clincher in a tight race, but Clinton is up to 15 points ahead of Republican challenger Bob Dole in opinion polls.
He doesn't need a foreign policy success nor the Jewish vote to win, pollsters agree.
Clinton's repeated commitment to the security of the Jewish state has earned him the reputation of being the friendliest president ever towards Israel.

This has not deterred Arab Americans from backing him, according to a poll Zogby conducted during the first week of October. Arab Americans, who make up about one percent of voters, prefer Clinton over Dole by the same 14 to 15 percent margin as nationally.
One reason for this popularity has been Clinton's efforts to keep Israeli-Palestinian peace on track.

"Foreign policy blipped on the radar screen during the summit," Zogby said, referring to the hastily convened White House meeting this month between Arab and Israeli leaders to salvage the Palestinian self-rule agreement, the cornerstone of U.S. regional policy.
"During the meeting there was a move towards Clinton over Dole but that was due to the publicity," he said.
Similarly, Clinton's lead jumped to 19 points after he ordered missile strikes against Iraq in September but the effect was shortlived.
The fact is that Arab and Jewish Americans, like most voters, are preoccupied with local issues.
"When presented with a list of 11 issues, voters put foreign policy last and that's not going to change," Zogby said.
The Middle East resonates more with Arabs and Jews but education, health care, crime, drugs, taxes and political integrity still rank above it, pollsters say.
"Unless there's something compelling overseas, a disaster or bombing, this is not going to change," Zogby said.
"The Middle East is a strong bipartisan area," said John Steinbruner, a foreign analyst at the Brookings Institution. "There's a decent consensus."

This has shown up on the campaign trail where the contenders have barely skirmished on foreign affairs. The Republicans have accused Clinton of "photo-op foreign policy", but the charge has not stuck with voters.
A recent USA TODAY/CNN/Gallup poll said voters thought Clinton would do a better job than Dole of handling foreign policy -- by 48 percent to 39 percent.
